body.text: On October 21, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, announced that loudspeakers for psychological warfare against South Korea would begin operations along the whole border before the end of the month, according to the North’s state-controlled Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). She made the announcement after inspecting fortification work at several border sites early that morning. The work followed a declaration by Kim Jong Un in late 2023 that the two Koreas were hostile states.

Pyongyang’s announcement about resuming the loudspeaker broadcasts came weeks after a land mine explosion in the southern border of the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on September 21. Two blasts injured three South Korean soldiers in the DMZ, which divides the peninsula. On October 5, South Korean and United Nations Command investigators concluded that North Korea had planted the mines in violation of the Korean War armistice. However, Pyongyang has rejected the finding. In fact, Kim Yo Jong described the blasts in her statement of October 22 as a suspicious accident that South Korea created for itself.

A mine blast has led to loudspeaker use before. In 2015, land mines injured two South Korean soldiers, and Seoul turned its speakers back on for the first time in 11 years. The two Koreas agreed in 2018 to stop the broadcasts and took down their speakers. Under then-South Korean President Yoon Suk-yeol, Seoul resumed broadcasts in June 2024 in retaliation for trash balloons flown from North Korea.

South Korean President Lee Jae-myung chose the opposite course after taking office in 2025. He halted the broadcasts and began dismantling the speakers that August. North Korea stopped its own broadcasts around the same time. The blasts of September have put that policy under strain, as Pyongyang has pledged to resume broadcasts.

So far, Lee has answered the landmine explosion – and North Korea’s denial – with diplomacy. On October 22, his government sent a letter to the president of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). The letter condemned North Korea for violating the armistice and called on Pyongyang to apologize. On October 25, North Korea replied with a letter of its own to the United Nations Security Council. The letter accused South Korean troops of firing warning shots at North Korean personnel and invoked the right of self-defense under the United Nations Charter.

In Seoul, the Defense Ministry ties its warning shots and broadcasts to a dispute over where the border line, formally known as the Military Demarcation Line (MDL), runs within the DMZ. On October 23, South Korea’s Defense Ministry proposed military talks to confirm where the MDL lies. The ministry had extended a similar offer in November 2025. Both times, North Korea ignored the proposal.
Instead, Pyongyang has decided to up the ante. Kim Yo Jong said North Korea’s resumption of loudspeaker broadcasts was retaliation for the South’s defense of the border.

While North Korea complains of “provocations” by the South, Lee is already under fire at home for not responding strongly enough. In an Armed Forces Day address on October 1, Lee expressed sorrow for the soldiers wounded in the landmine blast but did not blame North Korea. The leadership of the main opposition People Power Party (PPP) boycotted the ceremony in protest. On October 27, South Korean Unification Minister Chung Dong-young drew fire at a parliamentary audit for calling landmines defensive weapons.

Since then, the PPP has urged the government to restart loudspeaker broadcasts toward the North. Restarting the broadcasts would meet public demand for strong action against North Korea. Still, the move would undo the mutual halt that began in 2025. It would also let Pyongyang say that Seoul had started the loudspeaker war. As of this writing, the North Korean speakers are still silent, although locals reported hearing faint noises for four to five hours on the morning of October 29, in what Yonhap News Agency called “a test broadcast.”

Kim Yo Jong’s comments suggested that North Korea would resume broadcasts by October 31, the last day of the month. South Korea’s Defense Ministry has signaled that it would take a proportionate measure if the broadcasts begin. It has not specified what that measure would be.

Doing nothing has a cost of its own. Lee already faces accusations from the PPP that his government has deferred to North Korea. Talks would be the natural middle course, but Pyongyang has refused all requests for discussions. Nothing in the statements of Kim Yo Jong suggests that will change.

Instead, Pyongyang is seeking to impose its terms on the border unilaterally. Kim Yo Jong has cast the new North Korean fortification as a path to peace. According to her, a sealed border will lower the danger of military conflict. Her statement published on October 21 cited Kim Jong Un as wanting the border to be a lasting boundary. That leaves little hope that Pyongyang will agree to discuss the exact placement of the MDL with Seoul.

The loudspeakers are part of North Korea’s strategy. They are cheap for Pyongyang and force Seoul to respond. The older artillery that North Korea has placed in open view along its west coast serves the same purpose. On October 27, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff described the guns as legacy systems rather than new weapons.

The timing may serve Pyongyang as well. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit opens in Shenzhen, China, on November 18. U.S. President Donald Trump has raised the prospect of meeting Kim Jong Un on the sidelines, although more recently he has voiced uncertainty about such a summit. If tension along the DMZ eases before then, it could look like a concession to Trump.

While the tensions between the two Koreas have risen, Kim Jong Un made an unexpected one-day trip to China. Accompanied by Kim Yo Jong, he visited the border city of Dandong on October 24 and returned home the same day. Neither side announced the trip in advance. Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of the Politburo of the Chinese Communist Party, received him and conveyed greetings from Chinese leader Xi Jinping. No meeting with Xi was reported.

The trip came after several days of online rumors that Kim had died of a brain hemorrhage. In Seoul, the National Intelligence Service reportedly informed lawmakers on October 23 that the rumors were false.

Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said on October 27 that Kim and Chinese officials may have discussed talks with Washington. Cho also noted that Washington would prefer Seoul not to move too far ahead on potential North Korea-U.S. talks. North Korea official account of Kim’s trip mentioned neither talks with Washington nor the loudspeakers.

Whatever the motive, North Korea sets the tempo for engagement and tension alike, and Seoul can only react. Lee cannot ignore the loudspeakers, and every possible response – including no response at all – costs him something. Until Pyongyang agrees to talk, the Korean Peninsula is likely to drift toward more tension.

On a related note, Seoul’s JCS said on October 29 that North Korea fired a dozen of short-range ballistic missiles toward its east coast. According to the South’s military, the missiles were fired off from the Wonsan area around 12:30 p.m. KST, and flew about 250 km.
